# MULTI-REGIONAL SUPPLIER ONBOARDING & INTEGRATION STRATEGY
## Post-Tariff Nearshoring Transition (2025–2027)

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

**Strategic Context:** A consumer-electronics manufacturer is executing a rapid supply-chain rebalancing in response to 2025 tariff realignments and export-control expansions. Historical reliance on East Asian suppliers (cost-optimized, scale-proven, but geopolitically exposed) is being hedged with new suppliers in:
- **Mexico:** Nearshore manufacturing for North American logistics advantage; familiarity with US regulatory frameworks but limited electronics experience
- **Morocco:** Entry into North African/European supply corridor; nascent industrial base; strong government support but quality-consistency concerns
- **Vietnam:** Alternative to China/Taiwan geopolitical risk; experienced electronics workforce but new relationship-building required; language/cultural barriers

**Core Challenges:**

1. **Specification & Quality Misalignment**
   - Early audits reveal: Mexico suppliers interpreting tolerances as "targets" rather than hard specifications; Morocco partners unclear on lead-time criticality and change-request protocols; Vietnam manufacturers adapting designs without pre-approval (cost-optimization habit from prior OEM relationships)
   - Root causes: No shared quality-management language; differing assumptions about what "defect" means; inadequate pre-production communication of expectations

2. **Trust & Relationship Deficit**
   - Transactional first engagements create skepticism on both sides: Suppliers fear long-term commitment without guaranteed volumes; manufacturer fears quality/delivery disasters
   - Early miscommunications (e.g., Mexico supplier delays blamed on "supplier incompetence" vs. actual issue: unclear delivery windows, port congestion) erode goodwill
   - No established escalation channels for mid-production problem-solving; issues balloon into crises

3. **Communication & Cultural Barriers**
   - Language gaps: Mexico suppliers speak Spanish; Morocco team operates in French/Arabic/Darija; Vietnam workforce primarily Vietnamese
   - Work-style differences: Mexico operates via personal relationships + verbal agreements; Morocco expects formal government/bureaucratic protocols; Vietnam has hierarchical decision-making + limited upward feedback
   - Time-zone fragmentation: Mexico (UTC-6 to -8), Morocco (UTC+0), Vietnam (UTC+7) creates 14+ hour gaps; synchronous problem-solving difficult

4. **Quality-System Incompatibility**
   - East Asian suppliers operate via ISO 9001 + proprietary internal audits (mature SPC, documented lessons learned); Mexico suppliers operate ad-hoc inspection + rework loops; Morocco has limited SPC capability; Vietnam has ISO 9001 certification but inconsistent enforcement
   - No unified quality language: Defect classification, non-conformance escalation, root-cause analysis methods differ across suppliers
   - Testing protocols misaligned: Manufacturer specifies functional testing per IEC standards; Mexico supplier uses visual + manual checks; Morocco lacks equipment for advanced testing; Vietnam over-tests on some metrics, under-tests on others

5. **Volume Predictability & Capacity Planning**
   - Nearshoring paradoxically increases demand uncertainty: Mexico/Morocco/Vietnam suppliers ramping new production (first-time orders), causing yield variability, delivery delays
   - Manufacturer's demand forecasts (based on historical East Asian supplier lead times of 6–8 weeks) don't match new suppliers' actual lead times (Mexico 8–10 weeks due to port constraints, Morocco 10–12 weeks, Vietnam 7–9 weeks but high variability in first 6 months)
   - No capacity buffer: Early orders are "pilot" volumes (not yet profitable for suppliers), incentivizing them to prioritize existing customers or higher-margin orders

6. **Regulatory & Compliance Fragmentation**
   - Mexico suppliers required to comply with USMCA rules-of-origin (50% regional content threshold); manufacturer unfamiliar with certification process
   - Morocco partners must navigate European subsidy schemes + tariff-preference protocols; documentation requirements differ from East Asia
   - Vietnam manufacturers subject to anti-dumping regulations + potential US export-control reviews; unclear how proposed design changes affect HS code classification

**Strategic Approach (Four Pillars):**

1. **Structured Onboarding Framework** (3–6 months per supplier)
   - Pre-production validation phase: Joint design review, process capability studies, trial production runs
   - Documented quality agreements (signed by both parties): Specification clarity, defect definitions, acceptance criteria, change-request protocols, escalation procedures
   - Dedicated onboarding team (manufacturer + supplier) with clear roles, weekly syncs, shared scorecard

2. **Unified Quality-Management System** (Deploy across all new suppliers by Month 9)
   - Common defect classification language (adapted from IEC standards, manufacturer priorities)
   - Standardized SPC/process-capability documentation across Mexico/Morocco/Vietnam
   - Shared root-cause-analysis methodology (5-why framework, documented lessons learned)
   - Quarterly supplier conferences (virtual + in-person) to share best practices, benchmark quality metrics

3. **Communication Architecture & Cultural Adaptation**
   - Bilingual/trilingual documentation: Spanish for Mexico, French for Morocco, Vietnamese for Vietnam + English as business-standard "bridge" language
   - Asynchronous decision-making protocols: Issue escalation via shared tracking system (not real-time chat); 24-hour response SLA for urgent issues (enables regional participation without requiring synchronous overlap)
   - Dedicated liaison officers (manufacturer-based in each region or local hire) who speak language + understand business culture
   - Monthly executive business reviews (in-person for Year 1, quarterly after) to strengthen relationships beyond transactional problem-solving

4. **Collaborative Ramp & Volume Commitment Strategy**
   - Tiered volume commitments (binding for Year 1, minimum purchase guarantees) to incentivize supplier investment in tooling, training, capacity
   - Supplier development program: Joint training on IEC standards, SPC, design-for-manufacturability; manufacturer co-invests in equipment/capability if needed
   - Forecast transparency: 12-month rolling demand plan shared with all suppliers; 6-month frozen window for volume stability
   - Early-pay discounts + guaranteed profit margins (for first 2–3 years) to offset supplier risk of nearshoring transition

---

## PART 1: STRUCTURED ONBOARDING FRAMEWORK

### 1.1 Pre-Production Validation Phase (Weeks 0–16)

**Objective:** Confirm supplier's capability to meet specifications before any production order; identify process gaps; build mutual understanding of expectations.

**Phase Breakdown (with Gatekeeping):**

| Phase | Milestone | Duration | Key Activities | Deliverables | Go/No-Go Decision Gate |
|-------|-----------|----------|-----------------|---------------|----------------------|
| **Phase 0: Supplier Vetting & Capacity Assessment** | Supplier baseline capability confirmed | Weeks 0–3 | (1) On-site audit by manufacturer quality team (48-hour visit); assess: equipment, SPC maturity, quality documentation, workforce training, management commitment; (2) Capability study: Manufacturing process FMEA for key components, process-capability study (Cpk) on 3–5 production runs of similar products; (3) References check (2–3 existing customer interviews); (4) Financial health check (D&B report, bank references) | (1) Audit report (findings + risk areas); (2) FMEA documentation; (3) Process-capability baseline (Cpk scores); (4) Reference summary; (5) Financial report | **Gate 1 (Week 3):** Cpk ≥1.33 on all critical processes, zero major audit findings (or minor findings with corrective-action plan); financial health acceptable. If **No-Go**: Supplier removed from onboarding; restart vetting with alternative. If **Go**: Proceed to Phase 1. |
| **Phase 1: Joint Design Review & Specification Clarification** | Detailed specifications signed off; design verified for manufacturability | Weeks 3–8 | (1) Detailed design review with supplier manufacturing/quality engineering; confirm all tolerances, material specs, test protocols, packaging; resolve any ambiguities in drawings; (2) Design-for-manufacturability (DFM) review: Supplier recommends process method, tooling, lead times, yield assumptions; manufacturer validates feasibility; (3) Specification sign-off meeting: Both parties agree in writing on all specs, accept/reject criteria, test methods (IEC standards vs. proprietary), measurement equipment required; (4) Sample parts procurement: Supplier produces 20–50 sample parts per product family; manufacturer tests for conformance to spec | (1) Signed specification document (English + local language); (2) DFM report (supplier-drafted, manufacturer-reviewed); (3) Design-verification test report (samples tested per signed protocol); (4) Equipment qualification list (all measurement/test tools supplier will use, calibration status) | **Gate 2 (Week 8):** 95%+ sample conformance to specification; all DFM concerns resolved; equipment qualified. If **No-Go**: Iterate design/specs; restart Phase 1 with revised specs. If **Go**: Proceed to Phase 2. |
| **Phase 2: Process Capability Study & Trial Production** | Supplier process validated to produce consistent parts; trial quantities delivered on schedule | Weeks 8–14 | (1) Supplier runs trial production: 500–2,000 units per product (varies by volume/complexity); manufacturer quality team observes first-piece inspection + in-process checks; (2) Full statistical analysis: SPC data collected, process-capability indices (Cpk, Ppk) calculated for all critical parameters; trend analysis of yield/defect rates across trial run; (3) Defect-root-cause analysis: Any defects >5% of trial batch trigger joint root-cause investigation (5-why analysis); corrective actions documented; (4) Lead-time validation: Trial run completion timeline vs. promised lead time; logistics route tested (supplier → port → [destination port] → manufacturer); actual lead time documented | (1) Trial production run report (units produced, yield %, first-pass rate); (2) SPC data sheets + statistical analysis (Cpk ≥1.33 per critical parameter); (3) Defect/root-cause logs (if >0 defects); (4) Lead-time validation report (actual vs. promised, logistics route confirmed); (5) Quality auditor sign-off on process capability | **Gate 3 (Week 14):** Cpk ≥1.33 on all critical parameters; lead time ≤promised time ±10%; <2% defect rate on trial batch; all root-cause issues resolved. If **No-Go**: Extend trial run or iterate process; restart Phase 2. If **Go**: Proceed to Phase 3. |
| **Phase 3: Pilot Production Order & Continuous Improvement Plan** | First production order completed on schedule with quality metrics meet targets; improvement roadmap established | Weeks 14–16 | (1) Pilot production order (2,500–10,000 units, first month's actual demand volume) executed per signed specs; manufacturer conducts incoming inspection (100% for high-risk parameters, sampling for low-risk); (2) Defect tracking + real-time escalation: Any defect ≥0.5% rate triggers immediate joint problem-solving call; root-cause investigation + corrective action within 24 hours (escalation protocol in place); (3) Delivery performance: Actual delivery date vs. promised; logistics execution; inventory arrival at manufacturer's DC; (4) Kick-off of Continuous Improvement Plan: Supplier commits to quarterly SPC metric targets (Cpk increase +0.1 per quarter for 4 quarters); manufacturer commits to rolling forecasts, stable specifications; joint scorecards established | (1) Pilot production execution report; (2) Incoming inspection results (% passed per parameter, defect categories); (3) Delivery performance report (on-time %, lead time actual); (4) Continuous Improvement Plan (signed by both parties, 12-month roadmap with quarterly targets) | **Gate 4 (Week 16):** <1% defect rate on pilot order; on-time delivery achieved; Continuous Improvement Plan signed; supplier capacity confirmed for Year 1 volumes. If **No-Go**: Supplier enters probation (limited volumes, increased inspection) or removed. If **Go**: Full production ramp approved. |

**Onboarding Team Structure (Dedicated per Supplier):**

| Role | Reports To | Responsibility | Location | Cost |
|------|-----------|-----------------|----------|------|
| **Onboarding Program Manager** | VP Supply Chain | Owns onboarding timeline, gate decisions, stakeholder alignment; weekly team meetings; escalation authority for gate decisions | Manufacturer headquarters | 1.0 FTE (internal) |
| **Quality Engineer (Supplier-Facing)** | VP Quality | Design review facilitation, SPC oversight, defect root-cause analysis, measurement equipment qualification | Manufacturer HQ or supplier site (visits) | 0.5 FTE (internal) or external consultant (if capacity gap) |
| **Logistics/Supply Chain Analyst** | Director of Procurement | Lead-time validation, port/customs clearance assessment, routing optimization, capacity planning for volumes | Manufacturer HQ (remote coordination) | 0.5 FTE (internal) |
| **Supplier Account Manager (Local Hire or Expatriate)** | Onboarding Program Manager | On-ground presence at supplier; language capability; relationship building; daily issue escalation; audit observer | Supplier location (Mexico City, Casablanca, Ho Chi Minh City) | 1.0 FTE (local hire preferred, $40K–$60K/year + benefits) |
| **Quality Auditor (External)** | VP Quality | Third-party audit of supplier processes, equipment qualification, training adequacy; provides independent gate-sign-off | Supplier location (visits per phase) | External audit firm (~$15K–$25K per supplier for full onboarding) |
| **Translator/Cultural Liaison** | Onboarding Program Manager | Multilingual documentation; meeting facilitation; cultural protocol guidance (how decisions are made locally, relationship expectations) | Supplier location or remote (contractor basis) | 0.25 FTE ($25K–$35K/year if local hire) |

**Cost Estimate for Onboarding One Supplier (6-Month Cycle):**
- Internal staff (PM, QA, SCM): ~$60K (partially allocated to onboarding)
- External quality auditor: $20K
- Local account manager (6 months): $20K–$30K
- Translator/liaison (part-time): $6K–$9K
- Travel (on-site visits, team): $15K–$25K
- **Total per supplier: ~$121K–$154K**
- **For three suppliers (Mexico, Morocco, Vietnam): ~$363K–$462K**

### 1.2 Detailed Specification & Quality Agreements Framework

**Objective:** Create binding, unambiguous specifications and quality standards; minimize interpretation disputes; establish conflict-resolution protocols.

#### **Document 1: Detailed Specification & Acceptance Criteria Agreement (Signed Pre-Production)**

**Structure & Content:**

```
SPECIFICATION & ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA AGREEMENT
Supplier: [Name] | Location: [City/Country]
Product Family: [Product Code & Description]
Effective Date: [Date] | Revision: [V1.0, V1.1, etc.]
Signatory Authority: [VP Quality + Supplier VP Operations] (both required)

SECTION 1: PRODUCT SPECIFICATIONS
├─ 1.1 Functional Specifications
│   ├─ Electrical parameters (voltage, current, frequency, power consumption)
│   │   • Parameter: [e.g., Operating Voltage]
│   │   • Target: [e.g., 5.0V]
│   │   • Tolerance: ±[e.g., ±0.25V]
│   │   • Test Method: [e.g., IEC 61000-4-2 static discharge; multimeter measurement per SOP-QA-003]
│   │   • Sample size: [e.g., 100% of units or statistical sampling (AQL 0.65%)]
│   │   • Acceptance: [e.g., ≥95% units pass; ≥98% pass triggers process review]
│   ├─ Dimensional specifications (drawings, tolerances, material)
│   │   • Drawing reference: [CAD file version/ECN status]
│   │   • Critical dimensions: [List with tolerance stack-up analysis]
│   │   • Material specification: [e.g., Aluminum 6061-T6, Paint: Polyester TGIC per ASTM D3363]
│   │   • Test method: CMM measurement per GD&T protocol; SPC documentation required monthly
│   └─ Performance testing (reliability, thermal, durability)
│       • Test type: [e.g., Thermal cycling -10°C to +50°C, 1,000 cycles]
│       • Sample size: [e.g., 10 units per 5,000-unit batch]
│       • Acceptance: [100% of test units pass without degradation >5%]
│
├─ 1.2 Material Specifications & Traceability
│   ├─ Material certs: Supplier provides mill certs for metals, COO for critical components
│   ├─ Component sourcing: Single-source or approved alternatives listed
│   ├─ Conflict minerals: RoHS/REACH compliance documented; supply-chain transparency (tier-2 supplier info)
│   └─ Traceability: Lot/batch numbers tracked; quarantine procedures if sourcing changes detected
│
├─ 1.3 Workmanship Standards
│   ├─ Visual defects: No visible scratches >2mm, dents >1mm, discoloration, solder bridges
│   ├─ Assembly: All connections crimped/soldered per IPC-A-610 standard; no cold joints, excess flux
│   ├─ Packaging: Anti-static bags, foam inserts, protective tape per spec; damage inspection on 100% of boxes
│   └─ Documentation: Batch certs, test reports, signed-off first-piece inspection per box

└─ 1.4 Regulatory Compliance
    ├─ CE/FCC/RoHS certifications (if applicable)
    ├─ Safety data sheets for hazardous materials
    ├─ Conflict minerals declaration (annual)
    └─ USMCA rules-of-origin certificates (for Mexico); origin certs (for Morocco/Vietnam)

SECTION 2: ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA & DEFECT DEFINITIONS
├─ 2.1 Incoming Inspection (Manufacturer's Receiving)
│   ├─ High-risk parameters: 100% inspection (automated + manual per SOP-QA-004)
│   ├─ Low-risk parameters: Sampling per ANSI/ASQ Z1.4, AQL 0.65%–1.0%
│   ├─ Sample size: [n = per statistical table; e.g., for 5,000-unit lot, n = 125 units for AQL 1.0%]
│   ├─ Acceptance: Zero defects in sample (at AQL 1.0%) = lot accepted; 1 defect = inspect additional 200 units
│   └─ Rejection: Lot rejected if cumulative defects exceed AQL threshold; supplier charged for 100% re-inspection + rework
│
├─ 2.2 Defect Classification & Severity Levels
│   ├─ CRITICAL defects (lot rejection, 100% re-inspection required)
│   │   ├─ Safety hazard: Component poses electrical/physical injury risk
│   │   ├─ Non-functional: Unit fails core function test
│   │   ├─ Regulatory non-compliance: CE/FCC failure, RoHS violation, tariff-code mismatch
│   │   ├─ Catastrophic material defect: Cracking, corrosion, delamination affecting >5% of batch
│   │   └─ Acceptance: Zero critical defects tolerated; supplier must investigate root cause within 24 hours + implement corrective action within 5 business days
│   │
│   ├─ MAJOR defects (conditional lot acceptance with rework plan)
│   │   ├─ Functional degradation: Performance within spec but <95% of target (e.g., efficiency 92% vs. 95% target)
│   │   ├─ Cosmetic but visible: Scratches 2–5mm, discoloration on exposed surfaces, misalignment of labels
│   │   ├─ Assembly quality: Solder joints visually acceptable but marginal per IPC-A-610 Class 2
│   │   └─ Acceptance: Batch conditionally accepted if defect rate ≤2.0%; supplier investigates root cause within 24 hours; corrective action due within 10 business days; next batch monitored (100% inspection for 2 consecutive batches)
│   │
│   ├─ MINOR defects (batch acceptable; supplier improvement tracked)
│   │   ├─ Documentation missing: Batch certs incomplete but materials verified
│   │   ├─ Packaging damage: Inner packaging OK but outer box dented; contents verified undamaged
│   │   ├─ Label misprint: Non-critical information incorrect but product ID correct
│   │   └─ Acceptance: Batch accepted as-is; supplier tracked for trends (if 3 minor issues in 6 months, escalates to major issue requiring investigation)
│   │
│   └─ 2.3 First-Piece Inspection (100% Verification on First Production Batch)
│       ├─ Performed jointly by supplier + manufacturer QA at supplier site
│       ├─ Documentation: First-piece photos, measurement certs (CMM), electrical test results
│       ├─ Sign-off: Both parties sign FPI report; any discrepancies trigger engineering review before batch release
│       └─ Validity: Remains valid for next 5,000 units unless: (a) supplier changes process/equipment, (b) material supplier changes, (c) 90 days elapse without production (restart FPI)

SECTION 3: TESTING & MEASUREMENT PROTOCOLS
├─ 3.1 Equipment Qualification (Manufacturer specifies tools; Supplier procures & maintains)
│   ├─ CMM machine: Accuracy ≥0.002" (typical for electronics); calibrated quarterly per ASME B89.4.1
│   ├─ Multimeter/Power supply: IEC 61010 certified; calibration traceable to NIST; annual recalibration
│   ├─ Test chamber (thermal/humidity): Temperature control ±2°C; humidity control ±5%; monthly verification with certified standards
│   ├─ Oscilloscope (if signal testing): Bandwidth ≥[MHz required]; probe calibration per manufacturer specs
│   └─ Supplier certifies all equipment qualified before first production run
│
├─ 3.2 Statistical Process Control (SPC) Requirements
│   ├─ Monthly collection: Supplier collects >30 measurements per critical dimension/parameter per production run
│   ├─ Analysis: Supplier calculates mean, std deviation, Cpk; plots trend charts; identifies out-of-control signals
│   ├─ Documentation: SPC charts submitted to manufacturer by 15th of following month (digital format, Excel or MiniTab)
│   ├─ Targets: Cpk ≥1.33 for all critical parameters; if Cpk <1.33, supplier initiates process improvement (due in 30 days)
│   └─ Trending: Manufacturer reviews YoY Cpk trends; improvement expected (+0.1 per quarter for Year 1; then +0.05 per quarter thereafter)
│
└─ 3.3 Test Report Documentation (per Batch/Lot)
    ├─ All batches: Manufacturer receives batch test report signed by supplier QA within 2 business days of batch completion
    ├─ Contents: Batch ID, lot number, material lot trace, first-piece FPI sign-off, sample inspection results, SPC summary, any deviations from spec noted with root cause/corrective action
    ├─ Format: Standardized template (Excel/PDF, English version + local language if requested)
    └─ Archival: Manufacturer retains all test reports for 7 years (regulatory requirement); supplier maintains copies for 5 years minimum

SECTION 4: CHANGE MANAGEMENT & SPECIFICATION UPDATES
├─ 4.1 Design Changes by Manufacturer
│   ├─ Engineering change notice (ECN) issued with 30-day advance notice (minimum)
│   ├─ Impact assessment: Supplier assesses feasibility, tooling cost, lead-time impact within 10 days
│   ├─ Negotiation: If change impacts cost/lead time >5%, both parties negotiate cost-share or timeline adjustment
│   ├─ Implementation: After sign-off, supplier implements and validates new process via FPI before next production run
│   └─ Timeline: No production of changed item until FPI completed
│
├─ 4.2 Process Changes by Supplier
│   ├─ Supplier seeks approval for material changes, process switches, equipment upgrades (e.g., switching from manual assembly to automated)
│   ├─ Supplier submits change request (form SOP-CHANGE-001) at least 20 days before intended implementation
│   ├─ Manufacturer QA reviews within 10 days; approves, requests trial run, or rejects
│   ├─ If approved: Trial run performed (500 units) with full FPI/SPC validation before full production
│   └─ Unapproved changes: If discovered, batch placed on hold; material reviewed but not released; supplier charged for re-inspection
│
└─ 4.3 Specification Document Control
    ├─ Master copy: Manufacturer maintains; revision tracked (V1.0, V1.1, etc.)
    ├─ Release: Changes require both Manufacturer VP Quality + Supplier VP Operations signatures
    ├─ Supplier distribution: All suppliers receive updated spec within 5 days of release
    └─ Obsolescence: Old specs marked "obsolete"; suppliers confirm destruction of old prints within 10 days

SECTION 5: ESCALATION PROCEDURES & DISPUTE RESOLUTION
├─ 5.1 Issue Categories & Response Times
│   ├─ URGENT (production impact, safety concern)
│   │   ├─ Examples: Batch quality fail, contamination, on-time delivery miss, safety defect discovered
│   │   ├─ Response time: Supplier QA lead contacts Manufacturer QA + Account Manager within 2 hours (same-day notification)
│   │   ├─ Investigation: Joint virtual meeting within 24 hours; preliminary root cause within 48 hours
│   │   ├─ Corrective action: Implemented within 5 business days or batch quarantined (no shipment)
│   │   └─ Escalation authority: Supplier Plant Manager + Manufacturer Director of Supply Chain (if unresolved within 48 hours)
│   │
│   ├─ SIGNIFICANT (quality trend, minor delivery delay, process capability slip)
│   │   ├─ Examples: Defect rate trending toward limit, lead time extended by 3–5 days, Cpk dropping to <1.33
│   │   ├─ Response time: Email notification within 24 hours; investigation within 5 business days
│   │   ├─ Corrective action: Plan due within 10 business days; implementation within 30 days
│   │   └─ Review: Discussed in monthly business review (see Section 6.2)
│   │
│   └─ ROUTINE (documentation issues, minor cosmetic concerns, forecast updates)
│       ├─ Examples: Missing batch cert, packaging label misprint, demand forecast change
│       ├─ Response time: 5 business days
│       ├─ Corrective action: Implemented or plan submitted within 15 days
│       └─ Review: Discussed in quarterly scorecard review (see Section 6.3)
│
├─ 5.2 Root-Cause Analysis Protocol (5-Why Framework)
│   ├─ Trigger: Any URGENT or SIGNIFICANT issue automatically triggers RCA
│   ├─ Process: Supplier quality team (with Account Manager observation) identifies root cause via 5-why questioning:
│   │   Why did batch defect rate reach 3%? → Because solder temperature was high
│   │   Why? → Because temperature sensor failed
│   │   Why? → Because calibration expired & was not replaced
│   │   Why? → Because maintenance schedule not linked to equipment qualification SOP
│   │   Why? → Root cause: Process discipline gap in maintenance scheduling
│   │   Corrective action: Implement calendar-based maintenance alerts; add monthly equipment check to supervisor checklist
│   ├─ Documentation: RCA report (template SOP-RCA-002) includes: issue summary, 5-why tree, root cause, corrective action, timeline, owner, sign-off
│   ├─ Verification: Corrective action effectiveness checked in next 2 production batches (100% inspection for quality metrics)
│   └─ Closure: RCA closed by both parties only after effectiveness confirmed
│
├─ 5.3 Defect Liability & Rework Costs
│   ├─ Supplier responsibility: Supplier bears cost of:
│   │   ├─ 100% re-inspection of rejected batch (supplier pays inspection labor if outsourced)
│   │   ├─ Rework/scrap of defective parts (supplier charges own cost, no markup)
│   │   ├─ Expedited shipping of corrected batch (if original delivery timeline compromised)
│   │   └─ Root-cause investigation (supplier absorbs cost)
│   ├─ Shared responsibility (if ambiguous root cause):
│   │   ├─ Joint meeting within 48 hours to determine responsibility (e.g., material supplier defect vs. supplier's handling)
│   │   ├─ If both parties at fault, cost shared 50-50 by default (unless investigation clearly apportions blame differently)
│   │   └─ Agreement documented in RCA report
│   ├─ Manufacturer responsibility (rare):
│   │   ├─ If spec was ambiguous or test method was incorrect, Manufacturer acknowledges fault
│   │   ├─ Manufacturer covers re-inspection cost; supplier not charged for rework of compliant-per-original-spec parts
│   │   └─ Spec clarified to prevent recurrence
│   └─ Volume impacts:
│       ├─ If supplier misses delivery due to rework, Manufacturer may delay payment (interest-free, pending corrected batch arrival)
│       ├─ If repeated quality failures (>2 in 12 months), volume commitments reduced to minimum tier until performance recovers
│
└─ 5.4 Unresolved Disputes (Third-Party Mediation)
    ├─ If issue unresolved after 30 days of joint problem-solving:
    │   ├─ Either party can request neutral mediation (cost split 50-50)
    │   ├─ Mediator: Quality engineering consultant (mutually agreed) or industry-standard body (JUSE, IQPC)
    │   ├─ Mediation timeline: Mediator assesses issue within 10 days; recommends resolution within 20 days
    │   ├─ Binding arbitration (if mediation fails): Escalated to legal dispute resolution per contract; arbitrator's decision binding on both parties
    │   └─ Cost: Losing party bears full mediation cost (acts as incentive for good-faith negotiation)

SECTION 6: COMPLIANCE & AUDIT RIGHTS
├─ 6.1 Audit Rights (Manufacturer may audit supplier)
│   ├─ Scheduled audits: Bi-annual (twice yearly) comprehensive audits with 2-week advance notice
│   ├─ Unannounced audits: Allowed if quality concern surfaces (e.g., defect spike); Manufacturer provides 48-hour notice
│   ├─ Scope: Equipment maintenance, SPC documentation, material traceability, training records, corrective-action effectiveness
│   ├─ Remediation: Audit findings due within 30 days; corrective-action plan due within 60 days for major findings
│   └─ Cost: Manufacturer bears audit cost; supplier provides on-site resources (time, facilities)
│
├─ 6.2 Regulatory Compliance Verification (Annual)
│   ├─ Supplier confirms RoHS/REACH compliance annually; provides updated certs for materials
│   ├─ Conflict minerals declaration (for mineral-rich components): Annual attestation
│   ├─ USMCA compliance (Mexico only): Origin certs provided with each shipment; verified by Manufacturer
│   ├─ Tariff classification: Supplier confirms HS code per Manufacturer spec (if code changes due to design modification, supplier flags change within 10 days)
│   └─ Failure to comply: Shipment placed on hold pending compliance verification; Manufacturer may pursue alternative sourcing if issues unresolved within 30 days
│
└─ 6.3 Corrective-Action Status Tracking
    ├─ Corrective actions tracked in shared system (e.g., Salesforce or supplier-portal dashboard)
    ├─ Status updated monthly by supplier; verified by Manufacturer QA monthly
    ├─ Overdue corrective actions (past agreed due date) escalated to Account Manager + Plant Manager within 5 days
    ├─ Closure authority: Manufacturer QA confirms effectiveness before closure
    └─ Metrics dashboard: Shared monthly review of open/closed CAs, trends in root-cause categories (process discipline, equipment maintenance, training)

SECTION 7: TERM & RENEWAL
├─ Validity: This agreement remains in effect for [duration, e.g., 12 months] from signature date
├─ Renewal: 90 days before expiration, parties meet to
